body: Dyck, Morse & Zingales ('How pervasive is corporate fraud?', Review of Accounting Studies 2024) use Arthur Andersen's collapse as a natural experiment: in an average year ~10% of large US public companies commit (alleged) securities fraud (95% CI 7-14%), ~41% misrepresent financial reports (excluding clerical errors), and about two-thirds of frauds go undetected. Fraud destroys ~1.6% of equity value per year (~$830 bn in 2021). An earlier version estimated 15%. Their 2010 Journal of Finance paper ('Who blows the whistle') found detection mostly came from employees, media, analysts and industry regulators, with auditors and the SEC a minority (exact shares unverified here). Implications for a long-term portfolio: (1) with 20-30 holdings, expect 2-3 to have some misreporting at any time -- diversification and position sizing are fraud insurance; (2) audit sign-off is weak evidence; (3) journalists, short sellers, employees and lenders often see it first (Cobrapost/DHFL, FT/Wirecard, Muddy Waters/Luckin, Hindenburg/Nikola, Cooper/WorldCom). In India, add SEBI forensic audits and NSE/BSE surveillance as detectors; SME and small caps likely have higher rates (no reliable estimate).
sources: https://www.law.nyu.edu/sites/default/files/upload_documents/Adair Morse How Pervasive is Corporate Fraud.pdf
title: Base rates: how common is corporate fraud and who catches it
